ECE 6390

Grating lobes and the visible window

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how an eight-element line steered to 60° keeps one beam at half-wavelength spacing and gains a grating lobe at one-wavelength spacing.

A uniform linear array adds one unit phasor per element. With the line along z and θ measured from that axis, adjacent contributions differ by ψ = kd cos θ + β, where k = 2π/λ, d is the spacing in metres and β is the applied progressive feed phase. The normalized array factor |AF|/N = |sin(Nψ/2)/(N sin(ψ/2))| reaches one whenever ψ is a whole multiple of 2π, because every phasor then points the same way.

Real directions use only part of the ψ axis. As θ runs from 0° to 180°, cos θ runs from 1 to −1, so ψ sweeps the visible window β − kd ≤ ψ ≤ β + kd, a band 2kd wide centred on β. Steering to θ₀ sets β = −kd cos θ₀, which places ψ = 0 at θ₀. Any other multiple 2πm inside the window is another full-strength beam, called a grating lobe, at cos θ = cos θ₀ + mλ/d.

Keeping every other multiple outside the window requires kd(1 + |cos θ₀|) < 2π, or d/λ < 1/(1 + |cos θ₀|). Broadside steering allows spacing just under one wavelength; steering toward the axis tightens the limit toward one half wavelength. A grating lobe exactly on the window edge points along the axis, where the element pattern sets its strength.

Grating lobes send power toward unintended directions and receive interference from them. They are a sampling effect: elements spaced too far apart cannot distinguish directions whose path phases differ by a whole cycle. Ordinary sidelobes between nulls are a separate, weaker feature that tapering controls.

Example

Eight elements steered to θ₀ = 60° need d/λ < 1/(1 + 0.5) = 2/3. At d = λ/2 the window spans ψ/2π from −0.75 to 0.25 and contains only the main beam. At d = λ it spans −1.5 to 0.5; the multiple m = −1 lies inside, giving a grating lobe at cos θ = 0.5 − 1 = −0.5, or θ = 120°.

Practice

1. A broadside line (θ₀ = 90°) uses d = 0.9λ. Does it have a grating lobe? What changes if it is steered to θ₀ = 45°?

Compare d/λ with 1/(1 + |cos θ₀|) for each steering angle.

At broadside the limit is 1/(1 + 0) = 1, so 0.9λ keeps only the main beam. At 45° the limit is 1/(1 + 0.707) ≈ 0.586, so 0.9λ admits a grating lobe near 114°; scanning the same array away from broadside brings one into real space.

2. Why does adding elements at the same spacing narrow the main beam but leave a grating lobe in place?

Separate the peak positions, set by ψ = 2πm, from the peak widths, set by N.

Peak positions come from ψ = 2πm, which involves only d, λ and β. Increasing N narrows every coherent peak, including the grating lobe, but cannot move it out of the visible window. Only smaller spacing or less scan removes it.
